hints: Consider what would happen to future growth if both daughter cells became specialised and could no longer keep supplying new cells.
walkthrough:
Keep a source of dividing cells**
Cell E remains unspecialised and can continue to divide. Its descendants can differentiate into specialised tissues.

Link this to growth**
This continuing supply of cells allows the shoot tip to keep growing. Simply saying that it makes more meristematic cells does not explain the benefit requested.
Final answer: Keeping one daughter cell meristematic maintains a supply of cells that can divide and differentiate, allowing continued growth of the shoot tip.

hints: Look carefully at size and shape first - compare cell F with cell G, then G with H, then H with J. What has happened to length and to the large white space inside?
Now look for new walls - when one outline becomes two side-by-side outlines, that tells you a division has happened. Think about which way the new wall runs, along the length or across the width.
Track the vacuole and the nucleus as markers - which daughter cell keeps the large vacuole, and what happens to the smaller companion-type cell between H and J?
walkthrough:
Reading F to G as growth and vacuolation**
You can see F is a small square meristematic daughter cell with dense cytoplasm and a central nucleus. In G it has become tall and thin with a very large central vacuole pushing the cytoplasm and nucleus to the edge. That is elongation with vacuole formation, the first step in becoming a transport cell.

Reading G to H as a longitudinal division**
In H there are now two cells side by side inside the same outer outline. A new vertical wall has formed along the long axis. The left cell keeps the large vacuole and will become the sieve tube element, the right cell is dense with no large vacuole and will become the companion cell. So one cell has divided longitudinally into two different initials.

Reading H to J as further growth plus transverse division**
In J the left sieve tube cell is even longer and larger, still highly vacuolated. The right cell has now become two cells stacked one on top of the other, each with a nucleus. That means the companion cell initial has divided again, this time transversely, to give the two companion cells seen next to one mature sieve tube element.

Final answer: F to G: cell elongates / enlarges and a large vacuole forms; G to H: cell divides longitudinally to give a vacuolated developing sieve tube cell and a companion cell initial; H to J: developing sieve tube cell elongates further and the companion cell divides transversely to form two companion cells.

hints: Start from the job - sieve tubes carry sugary sap under pressure over long distances. What kind of shape and end-to-end arrangement would make a low-resistance pipeline?
Think about what would get in the way of flow inside a normal cell - nucleus, dense cytoplasm, organelles and complete end walls. What could be removed or opened up?
Focus on the end walls between elements stacked in a column - they are not solid, they have holes. How would holes help movement but still leave some wall material?
Remember the sieve element cannot live alone - how does its connection to the neighbour companion cell help it stay alive and load solute?
walkthrough:
Long hollow tubes for continuous flow**
Mature sieve tube elements are elongated and joined end to end to make an uninterrupted sieve tube. That creates a straight, wide pathway so assimilates like sucrose can move by mass flow from source to sink with minimal diversion.

Emptying the cell to reduce resistance**
A mature element has only a thin peripheral layer of cytoplasm, no nucleus and very few organelles. With almost no contents blocking the lumen there is much less resistance and maximum volume for sap. It can no longer divide or fully control itself, which is why it depends on the companion cell.

Sieve plates with open pores**
The end walls are perforated to form sieve plates with large pores. Sap can flow almost freely from one element to the next, so pressure-driven mass flow is maintained along the whole tube.

Strength plus intimate link to companion cell**
The remaining sieve plate wall still gives support and stops the tube collapsing or bulging under high hydrostatic pressure, and can be plugged with callose if damaged. Abundant plasmodesmata connect the sieve element to its companion cells for rapid transfer of sucrose and other molecules during loading and unloading.

Final answer: Elongated cells stacked to form long continuous tubes; little cytoplasm / no nucleus / few organelles to reduce resistance to flow and give more space for sap; sieve plates with pores allow easy mass flow from cell to cell with little barrier; sieve plates support the tube and prevent collapse / bulging under pressure; plasmodesmata between sieve element and companion cell allow rapid exchange for loading.

hints: Sieve elements have no nucleus and few mitochondria, yet sucrose has to be moved against a concentration gradient at sources and sinks. Which neighbour cell looks able to do the work?
Think about how sucrose enters the phloem at a leaf and leaves at a root or fruit - movement into and out of the sieve tube needs help. What transport process uses membrane proteins?
Active loading needs energy and a gradient - recall how hydrogen ions are pumped out and then allowed back in with sucrose. Where would the ATP and the proteins for this come from?
walkthrough:
Loading and unloading the pipeline**
Companion cells control movement of sucrose and other assimilates into the sieve tube at the source for loading, and out of the sieve tube at the sink for unloading. This sets up the high solute concentration needed for mass flow by osmosis.

Powering active co-transport**
Companion cells have many mitochondria and pump hydrogen ions out by active transport. The proton gradient is then used to bring sucrose in with protons through co-transporter proteins, a form of secondary active transport.

Keeping the sieve element alive**
Because the sieve element has no nucleus and little machinery, the companion cell with its dense cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria supplies ATP, proteins and metabolic control. Plasmodesmata allow these materials and signals to pass directly to the sieve element.

Final answer: Move sucrose into sieve tube at source for loading and out at sink for unloading; pump protons / hydrogen ions out to create a gradient for secondary active co-transport of sucrose; provide ATP and proteins to the sieve tube element and maintain its metabolism.
